items.prompt: A technology is on 'Trial' rather than 'Adopt.' What does that ring actually communicate to the rest of the team?
choices: It's forbidden to use anywhere
It's worth pursuing, and someone is using it on a real bounded project, but it isn't proven enough yet to be the default
It's identical to Adopt, just an older label
It failed and should never be tried again
items.explanation: Trial means real, bounded usage is underway and looking promising, but the team hasn't yet gathered enough production evidence to make it the default choice for new work — that's the difference between Trial and Adopt.
items.reference:
🧪 Assess: small spike, non-critical
🚧 Trial: real, bounded project
✅ Adopt: default for new work
⛔ Hold: proceed with caution

Why: each ring names a different amount of evidence the team has gathered, not a quality judgment about the technology itself.

items.prompt: A technology is on 'Hold.' What does that ring mean for a team that already has it running in one existing service?
choices: The existing usage must be ripped out immediately
Existing use is tolerated, but nobody should start anything new with it
It means the exact same thing as Assess
It's a formal ban enforced by tooling
items.explanation: Hold is a caution signal for new work, not an emergency rip-and-replace order — existing usage is tolerated while the team avoids expanding its footprint, which is a very different action than an immediate migration.
items.reference:
🧪 Assess: small spike, non-critical
🚧 Trial: real, bounded project
✅ Adopt: default for new work
⛔ Hold: proceed with caution

Why: each ring names a different amount of evidence the team has gathered, not a quality judgment about the technology itself.

items.prompt: Why does a radar separate entries into quadrants (Techniques, Tools, Platforms, Languages & Frameworks) instead of one flat list?
choices: So a practice like contract testing isn't compared apples-to-oranges against something like a cloud provider
Quadrants have no real purpose, they're purely decorative
To make the radar look more complicated than it is
Because rings alone can only apply to one category
items.explanation: Quadrants group entries by what kind of thing they are, so the radar doesn't force a comparison between fundamentally different categories of decision — a technique and a platform are evaluated on very different criteria even when both happen to be on 'Trial.'
items.reference:
🛠️ Techniques — ways of working
🧰 Tools — build/run support
🏗️ Platforms — what you build on top of
💻 Languages & Frameworks — code-level building blocks

Why: the quadrant answers 'what kind of thing is this,' the ring answers 'how sure are we about it.'

items.prompt: Trunk-based development and a new CI system are both being proposed for the radar. Which quadrants do they belong to, respectively?
choices: Both belong in the same quadrant, since both help delivery
Trunk-based development is a Technique; a CI system is a Tool
Trunk-based development is a Platform; a CI system is a Technique
Quadrants only apply to programming languages
items.explanation: Trunk-based development is a way of working (a Technique), while a CI system is software that supports building and running other software (a Tool) — different categories, evaluated on different grounds even though both could plausibly land on the same ring.
items.reference:
🛠️ Techniques — ways of working
🧰 Tools — build/run support
🏗️ Platforms — what you build on top of
💻 Languages & Frameworks — code-level building blocks

Why: the quadrant answers 'what kind of thing is this,' the ring answers 'how sure are we about it.'

items.prompt: In L1's opening scenario, how did the new framework end up in 3 of 11 services without anyone deciding it as a team?
choices: It was mandated top-down by a manager
One engineer adopted it locally, and others followed simply because it's what the last person to touch nearby code happened to know
It was the only option available
A formal committee approved it after review
items.explanation: Nobody made a team-wide call — the framework spread through local, uncoordinated decisions, each individually reasonable, that accumulated into de facto sprawl with no one place recording that it had happened.
items.reference:
🎤 One engineer sees it at a conference
📦 3 of 11 services quietly adopt it
🤷 Nobody can say if it's standard or experimental

Why: sprawl isn't one bad decision — it's many small, individually reasonable decisions with no shared record.

items.prompt: What specifically does a technology radar add that stops the kind of sprawl described in L1's scenario, without banning anyone from trying new things?
choices: A required approval committee that must sign off before any experiment
A shared, visible place to record what level of commitment the team actually has to each technology in use
A rule that only one technology per category is ever allowed
Nothing — sprawl is unavoidable regardless of process
items.explanation: The radar doesn't block anyone from experimenting (that's exactly what the Assess ring is for) — it makes the level of commitment visible and shared, so 'we're trying this' and 'we're standing behind this' stop being indistinguishable from the outside.
items.reference:
🎤 One engineer sees it at a conference
📦 3 of 11 services quietly adopt it
🤷 Nobody can say if it's standard or experimental

Why: sprawl isn't one bad decision — it's many small, individually reasonable decisions with no shared record.

items.prompt: Why does L1 treat 'a technology is hyped' and 'a technology is worth adopting' as different questions?
choices: They're the same question, just phrased differently
Hype reflects attention and excitement; adoption on a radar reflects actual evidence gathered through use on real work
Hyped technologies are always on Hold
Adoption always follows hype automatically within a few months
items.explanation: Hype is a signal about attention, not evidence — a technology can be genuinely exciting and still fail an Assess-ring spike, or be unglamorous and still be exactly right for Adopt. The radar exists specifically to separate those two things.
items.reference:
📣 Hype = attention and excitement
🧪 Radar ring = evidence gathered through real use

Why: conflating the two is exactly how ungoverned sprawl happens.

items.prompt: A technology has almost no conference buzz but has quietly powered a team's most critical service for two years with no major incidents. Where does it most likely belong on the radar?
choices: Assess, since nobody is talking about it
Adopt, since it has real, sustained production evidence backing it, regardless of how little attention it gets
It can't be placed on a radar without hype
Hold, because unpopular technologies are inherently risky
items.explanation: The radar ring tracks evidence, not popularity — two years of quiet, incident-free production use is exactly the kind of evidence that earns Adopt, independent of how much external buzz the technology has.
items.reference:
📣 Hype = attention and excitement
🧪 Radar ring = evidence gathered through real use

Why: conflating the two is exactly how ungoverned sprawl happens.

items.prompt: Does every technology on a radar eventually climb from Assess to Trial to Adopt, if given enough time?
choices: Yes, every entry eventually reaches Adopt
No — most things assessed never become trials, and most trials never become the default
Yes, but only for Languages & Frameworks
No, entries can only ever move downward, never upward
items.explanation: The rings are not a guaranteed one-way ladder — stopping at any ring is a normal, common outcome. Most things explored don't pan out, and that's the radar working as intended, not a failure of the process.
items.reference:
🧪 Assess
→
🚧 Trial
→
✅ Adopt

Why: a radar records evidence honestly, so most entries plateau or drop rather than climbing all the way.

items.prompt: Can a technology move directly from Adopt to Hold, skipping Trial and Assess entirely?
choices: No, it must pass back through every ring in order
Yes — a superseded option or a newly discovered problem can pull an Adopt-ring entry straight to Hold
No, Adopt-ring entries are permanent and can never change
Only if the team votes unanimously
items.explanation: Ring movement isn't bound to a fixed sequence — an entry can be pulled back to Hold from any ring the moment it stops earning its place, whether that's a security issue, an unmaintained upstream, or simply a better option emerging.
items.reference:
🧪 Assess
→
🚧 Trial
→
✅ Adopt

items.prompt: Is a technology radar meant to function as an approval gate that blocks engineers from trying new things?
choices: Yes, nothing can be tried without prior radar approval
No — it's a lightweight, shared record of commitment level, not a heavyweight approval process
Yes, but only for Platforms
It replaces all other technical decision-making entirely
items.explanation: The radar is explicitly described as lightweight and non-blocking — the Assess ring exists precisely so people can keep experimenting freely, with the radar simply making that experimentation visible rather than gatekeeping it.
items.reference:
📋 A radar = shared, visible record
🚫 Not a gate that blocks experimentation

Why: visibility, not approval, is what stops sprawl from becoming invisible.

items.prompt: What are the radar's two axes, and what does each one answer?
choices: Cost and popularity
Ring (how much commitment the team has) and quadrant (what kind of technology it is)
Team size and budget
Language and framework, only
items.explanation: The ring answers 'how sure are we about this?' and the quadrant answers 'what category of thing is this?' — together they let any entry be placed and compared meaningfully at a glance.
items.reference:
📋 A radar = shared, visible record
🚫 Not a gate that blocks experimentation

Why: visibility, not approval, is what stops sprawl from becoming invisible.

items.prompt: Two entries — a new database (Platform) and a new testing practice (Technique) — are both on the 'Trial' ring. Does sharing a ring mean they were evaluated the same way?
choices: Yes, ring alone fully determines how something is evaluated
No — they share the same commitment level, but sit in different quadrants because they're fundamentally different kinds of decisions
No, they must always be on different rings if they're in different quadrants
Quadrant and ring are the same thing
items.explanation: Ring and quadrant are independent axes — two entries can share a ring (same commitment level) while sitting in completely different quadrants (different kind of decision, different evaluation criteria).
items.reference:
💍 Ring = how sure are we
🗂️ Quadrant = what kind of thing

Why: the two axes are independent, which is what makes the radar a genuine 2D map instead of a single list.

items.prompt: A language (Languages & Frameworks quadrant) and a cloud provider (Platforms quadrant) both sit on 'Hold.' Does the shared ring mean the team evaluated them against the same criteria?
choices: Yes, ring alone determines the evaluation criteria
No — the ring only reflects shared commitment level (proceed with caution); the quadrant still determines what kind of criteria matter for each
No, entries in different quadrants can never share a ring
Ring and quadrant always move together
items.explanation: Ring and quadrant answer different questions independently — 'Hold' says both are currently discouraged for new work, but a language's evaluation criteria (syntax, tooling, hiring pool) and a cloud provider's (pricing, region coverage, compliance certifications) remain entirely different, because the quadrant, not the ring, determines what's being judged.
items.reference:
💍 Ring = how sure are we
🗂️ Quadrant = what kind of thing

Why: the two axes are independent, which is what makes the radar a genuine 2D map instead of a single list.

items.prompt: Per L2's lifecycle diagram, what has to happen before an entry can move from Assess to Trial?
choices: Nothing, entries can skip straight to Trial
A small, non-critical spike has to show enough promise that the dealbreaker question was answered favorably
It must first pass through Adopt
A vendor sales call
items.explanation: Assess is specifically for a small, non-critical spike whose job is to surface obvious dealbreakers — moving to Trial means that spike showed enough promise to justify running it on a real, bounded project next.
items.reference:
🧪 Assess → Trial: did the spike surface a dealbreaker?
🚧 Trial → Adopt: did it survive a real failure mode?

Why: each ring transition answers a specific, falsifiable question, not a vibe.

items.prompt: Per L2's lifecycle diagram, what evidence justifies moving an entry from Trial to Adopt?
choices: A real project ran it and survived an actual production failure mode, demonstrating the team understands its operational behavior
The Trial ring lasted at least six months, regardless of outcome
Someone on the team liked using it
It was mentioned favorably in a blog post
items.explanation: Adopt requires more than 'it worked in the happy path' — it requires evidence the team has seen and survived a real failure mode (an outage, a bad deploy, an on-call page) while using it, which is what separates confident, informed adoption from optimism.
items.reference:
🧪 Assess → Trial: did the spike surface a dealbreaker?
🚧 Trial → Adopt: did it survive a real failure mode?

Why: each ring transition answers a specific, falsifiable question, not a vibe.

items.prompt: A team ran a 2-day spike on a new tool and liked what they saw. Is that alone sufficient evidence to move it straight to Adopt?
choices: Yes, a positive spike is sufficient for Adopt
No — a spike is Assess-level evidence; Adopt needs real, bounded production experience via Trial first
Yes, as long as the spike lasted more than a day
No, spikes provide no useful evidence at all
items.explanation: A short spike is exactly what Assess is designed to produce — useful for surfacing obvious dealbreakers, but it hasn't been exposed to a real project's operational reality yet, which Trial is specifically for.
items.reference:
🧪 A spike ≠ production evidence
🚧 Trial is the step a spike can't skip

Why: skipping Trial means adopting on enthusiasm, not operational experience.

items.prompt: Why does skipping straight from Assess to Adopt reproduce the same failure mode as L1's ungoverned framework scenario?
choices: It doesn't — skipping Trial is always safe
Both cases commit the team based on enthusiasm and limited exposure rather than real operational evidence
Because Assess and Adopt are actually the same ring
Because L1's scenario had nothing to do with evidence
items.explanation: In both cases, commitment outruns evidence — one engineer's enthusiasm (L1) or one short spike's promise (skipping Trial) becomes the team's de facto standard without the operational proof that Trial exists to gather.
items.reference:
🧪 A spike ≠ production evidence
🚧 Trial is the step a spike can't skip

Why: skipping Trial means adopting on enthusiasm, not operational experience.

items.prompt: What question does the Adopt → Hold transition specifically ask, per L2?
choices: Has something changed — a better option, an unmaintained upstream, a security issue — that makes continuing to recommend it irresponsible?
Has the technology existed for over five years?
Did the original spike take too long?
Is the technology currently trending on social media?
items.explanation: Adopt → Hold is triggered by a concrete change in circumstances that undermines the original reasoning for adopting it, not by a vague sense of fatigue or a fixed time limit — the question forces a specific justification.
items.reference:
❓ Each transition = one falsifiable question
🚫 No question = 'loudest advocate wins'

Why: a question that can be answered wrong prevents ring changes from becoming pure opinion contests.

items.prompt: Why does L2 insist every ring transition point at an explicit, falsifiable question rather than a general sense of 'it feels ready'?
choices: Because without one, ring changes drift into 'the loudest advocate wins,' reproducing the hype-driven adoption the radar exists to prevent
Because falsifiable questions are required by law
Because it makes the radar look more technical
It doesn't matter, any justification works equally well
items.explanation: A vague 'it feels ready' has no way to be checked or disagreed with concretely — an explicit question ('did it survive a real failure mode?') can be answered yes or no with evidence, which is exactly what keeps ring changes from becoming a popularity contest.
items.reference:
❓ Each transition = one falsifiable question
🚫 No question = 'loudest advocate wins'

Why: a question that can be answered wrong prevents ring changes from becoming pure opinion contests.

items.prompt: Per L2's chart, why do most teams settle on a quarterly review cadence rather than monthly or annual?
choices: Quarterly is a legal requirement
It's frequent enough to avoid a whole release cycle of staleness, while infrequent enough to be a real scheduled conversation instead of constant noise
Monthly and annual reviews are both impossible to schedule
Cadence has no effect on how stale a radar becomes
items.explanation: The chart shows staleness rising steeply as review frequency drops — quarterly is presented as the practical middle ground between reviewing so rarely that entries silently rot, and reviewing so often that it competes with daily work for no real benefit.
items.reference:
📅 Quarterly = practical middle ground
📉 Annual/never = high staleness

Why: the radar's value decays with time exactly like any other cached decision.

items.prompt: What does L2 mean by 'the radar's value decays with time exactly like any other cached decision'?
choices: Radars physically expire and must be recreated from scratch each year
An entry's accuracy reflects the moment it was last reviewed, so an old, unreviewed entry can silently stop matching reality — just like a stale cache serving outdated data
Radars have nothing in common with caching
Only Platforms quadrant entries decay over time
items.explanation: A cached value is correct at the moment it's written and can silently drift out of sync with reality afterward — a radar entry works the same way: correct when last reviewed, and increasingly unreliable the longer it goes unrevisited.
items.reference:
📅 Quarterly = practical middle ground
📉 Annual/never = high staleness

Why: the radar's value decays with time exactly like any other cached decision.

items.prompt: A library on 'Adopt' has a critical CVE disclosed. The team's radar is reviewed yearly and the next scheduled review is 8 months away. What's the right response?
choices: Wait for the scheduled review, since consistency matters more than speed
Trigger an immediate, unscheduled ring change — security disclosures shouldn't wait for the calendar
Ignore it, since CVEs don't affect radar rings
Delete the radar entirely and start over
items.explanation: A radar needs both a routine cadence for ordinary drift and an out-of-band trigger for urgent events like a CVE or an upstream project going unmaintained — for 8 months, a purely calendar-driven radar would keep telling people 'this is the safe default' when it no longer is.
items.reference:
📅 Routine cadence: ordinary drift
🚨 Out-of-band trigger: urgent events (CVE, abandonment)

Why: a radar that only updates on schedule can actively mislead people between reviews.

items.prompt: Besides a security disclosure, what's another example of an event that should trigger an unscheduled radar update rather than waiting for the next cadence?
choices: An upstream project going unmaintained or effectively abandoned
An engineer taking a scheduled vacation
A minor version bump with no breaking changes
A typo found in the radar's formatting
items.explanation: An abandoned upstream is the same category of urgent, evidence-changing event as a CVE — it materially changes whether the entry's current ring is still honest, and shouldn't sit unaddressed just because the calendar hasn't reached the next scheduled review.
items.reference:
📅 Routine cadence: ordinary drift
🚨 Out-of-band trigger: urgent events (CVE, abandonment)

Why: a radar that only updates on schedule can actively mislead people between reviews.

items.prompt: Per L2's lifecycle diagram, what's required for an entry to move from Hold back to Assess?
choices: Nothing — Hold entries automatically return to Assess after a year
The team explicitly revisits it and confirms the condition that caused the Hold has actually changed
A single engineer's personal opinion that enough time has passed
Hold entries can never move again once placed
items.explanation: Moving off Hold requires an explicit revisit confirming the underlying condition changed — not just the passage of time or one person's hope, which is exactly the distinction L2's transition-question table draws for that row.
items.reference:
⛔ Hold → Assess: did conditions actually change?

Why: hoping conditions changed isn't the same as verifying they did.

items.prompt: A technology was put on Hold two years ago due to a licensing issue. An engineer wants to revisit it just because 'it's probably fine by now.' Is that sufficient to move it off Hold?
choices: Yes, time passing is sufficient justification on its own
No — the team needs to verify the specific licensing condition that caused the Hold actually changed, not just assume it did
No, entries placed on Hold can never be reconsidered
Yes, as long as the engineer is senior
items.explanation: 'Probably fine by now' is exactly the kind of unverified hope L2 warns against — the Hold → Assess transition specifically requires confirming the original condition changed, not just assuming time alone resolved it.
items.reference:
⛔ Hold → Assess: did conditions actually change?

Why: hoping conditions changed isn't the same as verifying they did.

items.prompt: In L3's scenario, three engineers each confidently recommend a different message queue. What does the scoring function actually do to resolve this?
choices: It produces one objectively correct answer that ends all disagreement
It forces the implicit disagreement about how much to weight each criterion into the open, where it can be argued about explicitly
It picks randomly among the three options
It eliminates the need for any human judgment at all
items.explanation: The three engineers weren't disagreeing about facts — they were weighting different criteria (scale, simplicity, operational burden) differently. The function doesn't manufacture agreement; it makes each person's implicit weighting explicit and arguable.
items.reference:
⚖️ Disagreement is about weight, not fact
💬 Scoring makes the weighting an explicit, arguable choice

Why: a score that hides its weights just launders opinions through arithmetic.

items.prompt: Two engineers run scoreCandidate with identical sub-scores but different weights and get different winners. What does that difference actually represent?
choices: A bug in the scoring function
A genuine disagreement about which criteria matter most to the team right now, made visible instead of hidden inside two people's unfalsifiable opinions
Nothing — the outcome should always be identical regardless of weights
Proof that scoring functions are useless for real decisions
items.explanation: With identical inputs, only the weights can explain a different outcome — that difference is the real, previously implicit disagreement about priorities, now visible and specific enough for the team to actually discuss rather than three people talking past each other.
items.reference:
⚖️ Disagreement is about weight, not fact
💬 Scoring makes the weighting an explicit, arguable choice

Why: a score that hides its weights just launders opinions through arithmetic.

items.prompt: L3 warns 'garbage in, garbage out' about the scoring function. What specifically is the garbage risk?
choices: The function's arithmetic is unreliable
If sub-scores are guessed rather than based on a real Assess-ring spike, the score just launders three people's opinions through arithmetic while looking more objective than it is
JavaScript can't handle decimal numbers correctly
The weights always sum to more than 1
items.explanation: The formula is only as honest as its inputs — sub-scores pulled from real spike evidence (per L2's Assess ring) ground the number in something real, while guessed sub-scores just dress up the same three opinions in a more convincing-looking wrapper.
items.reference:
🗑️ Guessed sub-scores = opinions in a number's clothing
🧪 Real spike evidence = an honest sub-score

Why: a formula can't fix bad inputs, it can only disguise them.

items.prompt: Per L3, when should a team run scoreCandidate over a set of options — before or after an Assess-ring spike?
choices: Before, so the score can decide whether a spike is even worth running
After, so the sub-scores reflect real evidence from using the technology rather than guesses
Timing doesn't matter at all
Only after full production adoption, never before
items.explanation: Scoring before any real usage means the sub-scores are just guesses dressed up as numbers — L3 is explicit that the score should follow a real spike, so the inputs reflect something the team actually observed rather than what they assumed going in.
items.reference:
🗑️ Guessed sub-scores = opinions in a number's clothing
🧪 Real spike evidence = an honest sub-score

Why: a formula can't fix bad inputs, it can only disguise them.

items.prompt: Two candidates score 5.6 and 5.9 out of a possible 10. Per L3, should the team treat that 0.3 gap as decisive?
choices: Yes, any numerical difference should always be treated as decisive
No — a gap that small is within the noise of subjective sub-scoring, and qualitative factors the formula can't capture should probably decide instead
Yes, because higher numbers are always unambiguously better
No, scores should never be compared at all
items.explanation: L3 explicitly distinguishes a real gap (like 4.3 vs. 5.9) from a close one (5.6 vs. 5.9) — a close score sits within the natural imprecision of subjective 0-10 sub-scores, so factors the formula can't capture (team morale, community responsiveness, a looming deprecation) should carry more weight in a near-tie.
items.reference:
📏 Big gap (4.3 vs 5.9) = a real signal
🤏 Small gap (5.6 vs 5.9) = noise, defer to judgment

Why: the score is a decision aid, not a tiebreaker precise to one decimal place.

items.prompt: Kafka scores 4.3 and NATS scores 5.9 in L3's worked example — a gap of 1.6. How does L3 characterize this gap compared to a 0.3 gap?
choices: Both gaps should be treated identically
The 1.6 gap is a real, meaningful signal; a 0.3 gap would be close enough that qualitative judgment should decide instead
A 1.6 gap is actually less meaningful than a 0.3 gap
Gaps have no interpretation in this framework
items.explanation: L3 draws an explicit line between a real gap worth trusting as a signal and a close one that's within the noise of subjective scoring — 1.6 points across four weighted criteria is a substantive, real difference, not a coin-flip margin.
items.reference:
📏 Big gap (4.3 vs 5.9) = a real signal
🤏 Small gap (5.6 vs 5.9) = noise, defer to judgment

Why: the score is a decision aid, not a tiebreaker precise to one decimal place.

items.prompt: L3's Checkpoint asks how the scoring would change at a company with a dedicated 6-person platform team and 50x the throughput. What would most plausibly change about Kafka's sub-scores in that context?
choices: Nothing changes — sub-scores are fixed properties of the technology itself
Its familiarity score rises (operational cost is amortized across specialists) and its strategic fit likely rises too (it's built for that scale)
Its maturity score would drop to zero
The weights would become irrelevant
items.explanation: Sub-scores describe the technology's fit for a specific team's real situation, not an abstract universal rating — a dedicated platform team changes the honest familiarity score, and much higher throughput changes the honest strategic-fit score, which is why the same formula can validly produce a different winner for a different team.
items.reference:
🏢 Small team, no infra staff → SQS wins
🏗️ Dedicated platform team, huge scale → Kafka may win

Why: the function isn't claiming one universal right answer — it's making the team's actual situation explicit.

items.prompt: Is it a flaw in the scoring approach if the same formula produces different winning candidates for two different teams evaluating the same three options?
choices: Yes, a correct scoring function must always produce the same winner
No — different teams honestly have different sub-scores (different familiarity, different strategic fit), so different winners are the function working correctly, not a bug
Yes, this proves the function is meaningless
No, but only because one of the teams must have made an error
items.explanation: The formula isn't claiming a single universal answer exists — it's evaluating each candidate against a specific team's honestly-scored situation. Two teams with genuinely different operational realities producing different winners is exactly what a well-built decision aid should do.
items.reference:
🏢 Small team, no infra staff → SQS wins
🏗️ Dedicated platform team, huge scale → Kafka may win

Why: the function isn't claiming one universal right answer — it's making the team's actual situation explicit.

items.prompt: Implement scoreCandidate(candidate, weights) exactly as described in L3: it returns the weighted sum of candidate.familiarity, candidate.maturity, candidate.migrationCost, and candidate.strategicFit, each multiplied by its matching key in weights.

tests.description: equal weights average the four sub-scores
tests.expr: expect(scoreCandidate({ familiarity: 4, maturity: 4, migrationCost: 4, strategicFit: 4 }, { familiarity: 0.25, maturity: 0.25, migrationCost: 0.25, strategicFit: 0.25 })).toBe(4)

tests.description: heavier weight on one criterion pulls the score toward that sub-score
tests.expr: expect(scoreCandidate({ familiarity: 10, maturity: 0, migrationCost: 0, strategicFit: 0 }, { familiarity: 0.7, maturity: 0.1, migrationCost: 0.1, strategicFit: 0.1 })).toBe(7)

tests.description: matches L3's worked Kafka score (within floating-point tolerance)
tests.expr: expect(Math.abs(scoreCandidate({ familiarity: 3, maturity: 9, migrationCost: 2, strategicFit: 5 }, { familiarity: 0.3, maturity: 0.2, migrationCost: 0.3, strategicFit: 0.2 }) - 4.3) < 0.001).toBe(true)

tests.description: matches L3's worked Hosted SQS score (within floating-point tolerance)
tests.expr: expect(Math.abs(scoreCandidate({ familiarity: 8, maturity: 8, migrationCost: 8, strategicFit: 6 }, { familiarity: 0.3, maturity: 0.2, migrationCost: 0.3, strategicFit: 0.2 }) - 7.6) < 0.001).toBe(true)

items.explanation: The score is a weighted sum: each sub-score is multiplied by its own weight and the products are added together. Because the weights sum to 1, the result stays on the same 0-10 scale as the sub-scores themselves, which is what makes candidates directly comparable.
items.reference:
➕ score = Σ (sub-score × weight)
⚖️ weights sum to 1, keeping scores on a 0-10 scale

Why: a weighted sum is the simplest structure that makes each criterion's influence explicit and adjustable.
